plain_language_claim: If you disagree with a WorkSafeBC decision on your claim, you can ask for a review within 90 days after the decision.
exact_quote_or_summary: Two search summaries gave slightly different wording: "Requests for review of compensation and assessment decisions must be submitted within 90 days after the decision." / "All requests to review claims and assessment decisions must be submitted within 90 days after the decision."
notes: Not confirmed verbatim (wording differs between summaries). Same 90-day period in Workers Compensation Act Part 6 per summary. Late requests may be considered if reasons are given (summary). Reconsideration within 75 days is not used on pages. Added for the coverage guide denied-claim section.

plain_language_claim: Form 6A is a notice of injury that a worker gives to their employer, not to WorkSafeBC; the employer may ask the worker to fill it in.
exact_quote_or_summary: Summary of the form page: the form is for the employer, not WorkSafeBC ("submit this form to your employer and not to WorkSafeBC", search-summary wording, not confirmed verbatim). Current page title in results: "Worker's Notice to Employer of Injury or Occupational Disease".
notes: Older title: Worker's Report of Injury or Occupational Disease to Employer (research/05 lists revision R26/07). Older policy PDF summary: worker must complete the Board form if the employer asks and the worker is able. Link to the form page; do not reproduce the form. Keyword: worksafebc form 6a.

plain_language_claim: Workers can contact the Workers' Advisers Office for advice at any stage of a claim.
exact_quote_or_summary: Search summary quoting the workers' claims review and appeal guide: "You can contact the Workers' Advisers Office for advice at any stage in your claim."
notes: Guide PDF not opened. The Workers' Advisers Office is separate from WorkSafeBC. Do not call the advice free unless confirmed.

plain_language_claim: Since January 1, 2024, workers and employers in BC have a legal duty to cooperate with each other, and with WorkSafeBC, in a timely and safe return to work.
exact_quote_or_summary: "starting on January 1, 2024, employers and workers have a legal duty to cooperate in timely and safe return to work" (health care providers RTW page). Return to work page summary: duty to cooperate with each other and with WorkSafeBC.
notes: Bill 41 amendments to the Workers Compensation Act. Worker fact sheet summary: duty applies to accepted claims with a date of injury on or after January 1, 2022. Page copy should not add other conditions.

plain_language_claim: Under the duty to cooperate, a worker must contact their employer as soon as practicable after the injury, keep in touch, help find suitable work when asked, give WorkSafeBC the return-to-work information it asks for, and not unreasonably refuse suitable work. WorkSafeBC can reduce or suspend wage-loss benefits if a worker does not cooperate without a reasonable reason.
exact_quote_or_summary: Summary of the workers duty page and worker fact sheet (Workers Compensation Act s. 154.2(2) and (6)). No verbatim sentence captured. Fact sheet summary: WorkSafeBC first assesses whether the reasons are reasonable; health care continues; benefits can be reviewed if the worker cooperates later.
notes: Contact requirements do not apply where contact would likely imperil or delay recovery (s. 154.2(3), summary). Refusing unsafe work under OHS rules is a separate right; do not mix them.

plain_language_claim: Under the duty to cooperate, an employer must contact the injured worker as soon as practicable, keep in touch with the worker and WorkSafeBC, and give WorkSafeBC the return-to-work information it asks for.
exact_quote_or_summary: Summary of the employer fact sheet: employers must reach out to the worker promptly, stay in contact with the worker and WorkSafeBC, offer suitable work and report return-to-work information to WorkSafeBC. WorkSafeBC can apply administrative penalties (s. 154.5, summary).
notes: Use with RTW-04 for the suitable work part.

plain_language_claim: Under the duty to cooperate, an employer must identify and make available suitable work that is safe, productive, within the worker's functional abilities and consistent with their skills.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); employer fact sheet (page date not shown)
exact_quote_or_summary: "Identify and make available suitable work that is safe, productive, within the worker's functional abilities, and consistent with their skills and competencies."
notes: Same definition of suitable work appears in the Rehabilitation Services and Claims Manual Vol. II C5-33.00 (summary).

plain_language_claim: An employer that regularly employs 20 or more workers, and employed the injured worker for at least one year before the injury, has a duty to maintain that worker's employment: it must offer the pre-injury job or a comparable one if the worker is fit for it, or else the first suitable work that becomes available, and accommodate up to undue hardship.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); in force January 1, 2024
exact_quote_or_summary: "If an employer regularly employs 20 or more workers and has employed the injured worker for at least one year before their injury, the employer has an obligation to maintain that worker's employment." "If a worker is fit to return to their pre-injury work, the employer is required to offer either that pre-injury work or a comparable alternative." "If the worker cannot perform their pre-injury job, but is otherwise fit to work in another capacity, the employer must offer the first suitable work that becomes available."
notes: Applies to claims with injury dates from July 1, 2023 (summary). Employer guidance words the service test as 12 continuous months full or part time. Page copy should name both conditions and say "may" for an individual reader.

plain_language_claim: WorkSafeBC does not require medical approval for a worker to return to work, but a written return-to-work plan can help keep the worker's health care provider up to date.
exact_quote_or_summary: "Although WorkSafeBC doesn't require medical approval for you to return to work, a written plan can help to update your health care provider on your progress, if needed."
notes: Employer page carries the same point. Do not turn this into "you do not need to see a physio".

plain_language_claim: A return-to-work plan is made by the worker and employer together; a WorkSafeBC team member, the worker's health care provider or a union representative may also be involved. The plan sets out the worker's functional abilities, job duties and hours of work.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); RTW Plan template revision R25/06
exact_quote_or_summary: "The plan is developed collaboratively by the injured worker and their employer (e.g., a supervisor, RTW coordinator, and/or others). A WorkSafeBC team member, the injured worker's health care provider, or a union representative could also be involved." "A RTW plan includes the worker's functional abilities, job duties, and hours of work."
notes: Page attribution between the template and the employer page comes from search results. WorkSafeBC asks employers to send a copy of the completed plan (summary).

plain_language_claim: Each version of a return-to-work plan is based on what the worker can safely do at that time, and a new version is made as the worker can do more.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); RTW Plan template revision R25/06
exact_quote_or_summary: "Each version of this plan is based on what you can safely do at a given time. We can begin with a plan for the first few days. As you can do more, we will create a new plan to reflect the progression."
notes: Basis for "gradual return to work". No duration is stated as a rule; do not add week counts (an employer guide summary mentions a typical length; not used).

plain_language_claim: A return-to-work plan gets a new version when duties change, including when the planned duties are not working out; if there are concerns about the worker's function or safety, a health care provider should be involved to review the plan.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); RTW Plan template revision R25/06
exact_quote_or_summary: Search summary of the template: a new version is needed "when their duties can be expanded or if the planned duties are not working out"; if there are concerns about the employee's function or safety, a health care provider should be involved to review the plan or give input on abilities. Not confirmed verbatim.
notes: Used for the warning-signs section: the plan can change.

plain_language_claim: WorkSafeBC asks workers to talk with their health care provider about activities they can do at work and at home and activities to avoid, then share this with their employer and discuss changing duties or adjusting their schedule so they can keep working.
exact_quote_or_summary: "Depending on the nature of your injury, talk to your health care provider about activities you can do at work and/or at home, as well as activities you should avoid. Share this information with your employer and discuss ways you might change your duties or adjust your schedule to be able to continue working."
notes: Manage a claim page has a similar line: "Ask your health care providers to recommend activities you can do to help your recovery, and those you need to avoid."

plain_language_claim: WorkSafeBC does not require a health care provider's approval for a worker to return to work; providers can help the worker see how their functional abilities connect to safe and suitable job duties.
exact_quote_or_summary: "WorkSafeBC doesn't require a provider's approval for a worker to return to work, you can support the worker and help them recognize the connection between their functional abilities and possible safe and suitable job duties at work."
notes: Same page (summary): WorkSafeBC may ask providers to run a return-to-work meeting, visit a jobsite or assess function against the pre-injury job; abilities-focused language. Do not imply Synergy does jobsite visits.

plain_language_claim: WorkSafeBC says returning to work might mean doing alternate tasks, working a modified schedule, or approaching things a little differently.
exact_quote_or_summary: "Returning to work might mean doing alternate tasks, working a modified schedule, or approaching things a little differently."
notes: Page attribution (Return to work page) from search summary. Basis for the "modified duties" definition.

plain_language_claim: WorkSafeBC suggests employers consider temporarily changing the worker's usual duties, days or hours, removing or reorganizing tasks, and allowing stretch breaks and rest periods.
source_date_or_retrieved: Retrieved 2026-11-02 (WebSearch snippet, allowed_domains worksafebc.com); Managing a Safe Return to Work guide dated 07/25
exact_quote_or_summary: "Consider: temporarily modifying their pre-injury duties, temporarily modifying their days and/or hours of work, removing or reorganizing tasks, and allowing for stretch breaks and rest periods"
notes: Exact page (employer page or guide) not pinned; both listed.

plain_language_claim: Wage-loss benefits can continue when a worker returns on reduced hours or different duties; WorkSafeBC takes the worker's earnings into account and may pay part of the difference.
exact_quote_or_summary: "We will subtract your net employment income from your net weekly wage-rate and you may be entitled to 90% of the difference." The link to reduced hours or different duties is from the search summary.
notes: Do not print the percentage on worker pages without staff check. Coverage of individual cases depends on the claim.

plain_language_claim: A worker's WorkSafeBC case manager is their main contact; the case manager manages the claim, decides benefits and helps the worker access services.
exact_quote_or_summary: Summary: the case manager is the worker's main contact, determines benefits, helps access services and manages the claim on an ongoing basis; works with the employer and providers.
notes: Some claims are handled by other WorkSafeBC staff; keep copy general ("your case manager or the WorkSafeBC officer on your claim" if needed).

plain_language_claim: If a worker and employer cannot resolve a disagreement about the duty to cooperate, WorkSafeBC can decide whether each has complied.
exact_quote_or_summary: Summary: the Board decides compliance disputes only if the parties cannot resolve them otherwise (Workers Compensation Act s. 154.2(4)). No verbatim sentence captured.

plain_language_claim: The warning-signs wording on the return-to-work article is Synergy clinical guidance, not a WorkSafeBC fact: some extra soreness is common when hours or tasks are added and often settles with rest by the next day; the listed signs (pain building from shift to shift or week to week, pain not settled by the morning after a shift, new numbness or tingling, weakness or a joint giving way, night or rest pain, new swelling, redness or heat, limping or guarding, a planned task harder than expected) should be reported to the physio; and the listed red flags (sudden arm or leg weakness, chest pain, trouble breathing, groin or inner-thigh numbness, new bladder or bowel control trouble) mean calling 911 or going to emergency.

Goldfish check egm/article-check-guide.md section 4, L188-194 item (b); SYN-09 note lists 'services WorkSafeBC does not cover' as an exception. Ops to confirm with Q-5. Contracted clinics may not charge extra for services under the agreement (WSBC-24), so this covers only services outside it.

plain_language_claim: The job-focused physio wording on the return-to-work article is Synergy clinical guidance, not a WorkSafeBC fact: physio goals can be set around your job tasks; your physio can look at what your job asks of your body and set treatment goals around those tasks, adding weight, time or reps a little at a time as you cope; your physio can keep working on your strength while you build up your shifts, and work on the hardest parts of your job before that last step; the listed job demands (lifting and carrying, standing, stairs, kneeling and squatting and walking, reaching and overhead work, grip and tools, sitting, driving and screen work, balance and footing at work); your physio may give you exercises to keep up at home between visits; and real detail helps your physio plan treatment around your job.
